title: Boosting the participation ratio during our explanations
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton follows up his earlier piece on the participation ratio by turning to the phase of the lesson teachers said they most needed to fix: explanations and worked examples. He starts with a warning against filling an explanation with questions about brand-new content, which turns it into a guessing game. He then offers five alternatives: check for listening, question only prerequisite knowledge that has just been assessed, model in silence with Silent Teacher, run a Step by Step whole-class check on mini-whiteboards, and finish with Adam Boxer's Tick Trick. The common thread is that every device makes it hard for a student to disengage unnoticed while also showing the teacher exactly where understanding breaks down. The post closes with reflection prompts for readers.
points: Questioning students about content they have not yet learned makes explanations slow and confusing, so questions should target listening and secure prior knowledge instead.
Students who know listening will be checked have a built-in reason to attend, which makes the checks double as an incentive.
Silent Teacher only works if it is followed by announced whole-class checks, since silence alone lets minds wander.
Step by Step and the Tick Trick both locate the precise step at which a student goes wrong, rather than just flagging a wrong final answer.
The Tick Trick also forces students to compare their own working line by line with a model, which reinforces the expected layout of solutions.
quotes: An obvious way to boost the participation ratio is to ask students lots of questions during an explanation or worked example. But we need to be careful what we ask them questions about.

If our students are not paying attention, then it does not matter how clear our explanation is as they will not understand it. The simplest check for listening is to ask students to repeat something you have just said.

Now, we only want to do this if we have recently assessed that prerequisite knowledge and have evidence that it is secure. If we don't, then we run the risk that we ask students a question that we assume they know the answer to, but it turns out they don't, and then we are forced to pause our explanation or worked example and intervene.
For those not familiar, this is where I model the worked example in silence, pausing at key points to challenge my students to consider: What has he just done? What do I think he will do next?

The first of these whole-class checks for understanding following the worked example is called Step by Step. Here, I give my students a problem to solve that is of a similar difficulty to the worked example, but first I ask them to just write the first step on their mini-whiteboards.
Following Step by Step, I want to see if students can solve a similar problem on their own from start to finish. I ask them to do this on their mini-whiteboards and show me when I ask.
